_note: Frozen content for design review. Editorial-lesson family — one principle per page with a callout.
brief: Design principles I wish someone had told me earlier

slots.body: Six principles that fixed more of my work than any tool or plugin ever did.

slots.title: If everything is emphasised, nothing is
slots.body: Bold, colour, size and motion all compete for the same attention budget. Spend it once per screen and the screen finally works.
slots.calloutBody: Pick the one element the reader must see, then weaken everything around it.

slots.title: Whitespace is not wasted space
slots.body: Crowding is what makes an interface feel cheap. Room around an element is what tells the eye the element matters.
slots.calloutBody: Double the space around your most important block before you touch anything else.

slots.title: Contrast carries more than colour
slots.body: Scale, weight and density separate things far more reliably than hue, and they survive being screenshotted, printed or read in sunlight.
slots.calloutBody: Turn the design greyscale. If the hierarchy vanishes, colour was doing the work.

slots.title: Alignment is invisible until it is wrong
slots.body: Nobody praises a clean grid, but everyone feels a broken one. Most designs that look amateur are just misaligned by a few pixels.
slots.calloutBody: Draw one line down the left edge of the layout and make everything meet it.

slots.title: Repetition beats novelty
slots.body: A system that repeats reads as intentional. A screen where every element is invented fresh reads as noise, however good each piece is.
slots.calloutBody: Reuse a spacing value and a corner radius everywhere before inventing a new one.

slots.title: Type does most of the work
slots.body: Before the illustration, the gradient or the animation, the typography decides whether the thing feels considered or thrown together.
slots.calloutBody: Fix the type scale first and half your layout problems disappear on their own.

slots.body: Not all six. Pick the one your current project breaks most often and hold the line on it until it is habit.
